findings.description:
`set_pending_rewards` and `allocate` mutate global reward-backing state and per-owner unit balances without any `require_auth` or other caller restriction. If this module is ever exposed via public entrypoints (e.g., future integration/feature-flag mistakes), any account could (a) clear or set the `pending_rewards` gate to unblock/lock redemptions and alter funding mode checks, and/or (b) allocate unallocated units to arbitrary owners, manipulating reward distribution.

Exploit path (if exposed): attacker calls `set_pending_rewards(env, 0)` to bypass the “unsettled backing rewards” gate in `redeem_with`, then calls `allocate` to redirect units, affecting who can redeem backing value.

Current mitigations/limits: this module is behind `#[cfg(any(test, feature = "hybrid-rewards"))]` and `hybrid-rewards` hard-errors on `wasm32`, so it should be non-deployable in production builds; impact is therefore contingent on future changes or misconfiguration.
findings.recommendation: If/when this code is ever made callable on-chain, gate all state-mutating functions (`set_pending_rewards`, `allocate`, and any funding/finalization hooks) behind a dedicated coordinator/admin authorization check (e.g., stored `Coordinator` address + `require_auth`). Consider keeping these functions non-public and only callable from validated internal entrypoints.
findings.title: Coordinator hooks callable without any authorization

findings.description:
Each distinct `owner` allocated units gets a persistent storage entry (`BackingKey::HybridBackingOwner(owner)`), and `set_owner` intentionally preserves even zero-value records. If `allocate` is ever callable by untrusted users (see missing auth finding), an attacker can create arbitrarily many persistent entries by allocating minimal units to many fresh addresses, growing contract state across transactions.

Exploit path (if exposed): attacker funds small amounts to create `unallocated_units`, then repeatedly calls `allocate` with new random `Address` values, forcing persistent writes + TTL extensions for each new key.

Practical impact is limited by Soroban fees/rent paid by the attacker and the fact the contract doesn’t iterate over all owners, but it can still bloat long-lived state.
findings.recommendation: If this becomes on-chain callable, restrict allocation to an authorized coordinator and/or enforce limits (e.g., only allow allocating to addresses present in a verified epoch ledger, or require nonzero allocations only for known participants). Consider deleting owner keys when balance reaches zero (if consistent with desired accounting invariants).
findings.title: Unbounded persistent owner records can be created

findings.description:
Several security-relevant configuration flags are stored in **instance storage** (`MinCashReserveBps`, `ClCustody`, `ClCustodyContext`, `CashBorrowingEnabled`), but this module never bumps instance-storage TTLs (no `env.storage().instance().extend_ttl(...)` anywhere). In Soroban, instance entries can expire independently of persistent entries; once expired, reads fall back to defaults (`None` / `false`).

If the contract relies on these flags for safety properties, their expiry can silently change market behavior without admin action. A concrete example is `ClCustody` (custody-only market mode): `deposit_into_boosted` explicitly forbids boosted-vault interaction when `cl_custody` is true, but if `ClCustody` expires it will read as `false` and the contract may start executing non-custody code paths for a custody-configured market, potentially moving assets into a boosted vault or enabling flows that were meant to be permanently disabled for custody markets.

Because this is a time-based state-loss vector that can flip critical configuration, it can lead to fund-loss or broken accounting once the instance TTL is reached, and can be triggered simply by letting the market sit idle past TTL (no attacker privileges required).
findings.recommendation: Add explicit instance TTL maintenance for any instance keys that must persist for the contract lifetime (e.g., a `bump_instance_ttl(env)` helper called by `ensure_initialized` and any other frequent entrypoints), or move these configuration flags to persistent storage if they are intended to be durable. Ensure any custody-mode invariants cannot be silently disabled by missing instance state.
findings.title: Instance config flags can expire and disable safeguards

findings.description:
`settle_one_recycled` and `compound` perform external swaps via `strategy.hybrid_swap` with `minimum` hardcoded to `1`, meaning any caller can trigger reward-token conversion at arbitrarily bad execution prices (including during manipulated AMM conditions). If this module were ever enabled in a deployable WASM build (e.g., by removing the current `compile_error!` gate for `hybrid-rewards` on `wasm32`), an attacker could front-run/back-run the permissionless `recycle`/`compound` flows to force conversions at extreme slippage, effectively extracting value from protocol rewards into the AMM and reducing rewards for all holders.

Note: In the current repository configuration, `reward_settlement` is only compiled for tests or non-wasm builds (`#[cfg(any(test, feature = "hybrid-rewards"))]`), and `hybrid-rewards` is explicitly blocked on `wasm32` (`compile_error!` in `src/lib.rs`). So this is not exploitable in the deployed ReceiptVault as-is, but is a high-risk footgun if the feature gate is changed.
findings.recommendation: If this logic is ever deployed on-chain, add caller-provided slippage bounds (min-out) to permissionless swap-triggering entrypoints (or restrict who can call them), and consider using a time-weighted price/quote check from a trusted oracle/DEX router to reject pathological execution. Avoid hardcoding `minimum = 1` for conversions that affect user value.
findings.title: Permissionless reward swaps lack slippage bounds

findings.description:
`redeem_with` calls `ledger::allocate` for each registered reward asset using `owner` provided as a parameter. `ledger::allocate` internally calls `checkpoint`, which persists a `HybridAccount(asset, owner)` record even when the owner has zero ReceiptVault balance (weight = 0) and even when `amount == 0`. If `redeem`/`redeem_with` were ever exposed as a permissionless entrypoint (or reachable without first authenticating the `owner`), an attacker could call it with many arbitrary `Address` values to create unbounded persistent storage entries, increasing contract rent/footprint and potentially causing DoS via state growth.

Note: As with the other hybrid reward modules, this code is currently not included in deployable `wasm32` builds (feature-gated and compile-error blocked), so it is not exploitable in production as-is.
findings.recommendation: If this code is ever deployed, require `owner.require_auth()` (or equivalent strong authorization) before persisting any per-owner accounting, and/or avoid creating/persisting ledger accounts when `weight == 0` and no state existed previously. Consider explicit bounds/allowlists on who can trigger allocation for third parties.
findings.title: Arbitrary owner parameter can bloat ledger storage

findings.description:
`utilization()` returns `0` when `denom == 0` (i.e., `cash + borrows == reserves`), which represents a 100% reserve share / undefined utilization edge case. Returning 0 makes `get_borrow_rate` fall back to ~`base_rate`, dramatically *lowering* rates exactly when the pool is most stressed.

Exploit path (economic): if protocol state can reach `pooled_reserves == cash + borrows` (e.g., large accumulated reserves/admin fees plus cash drained via withdrawals while borrows remain), subsequent interest accrual in `ReceiptVault::update_interest` that queries this model will compute a near-minimum borrow rate, undercharging borrowers and harming lenders/protocol accounting until the condition clears.
findings.recommendation: Handle `denom == 0` explicitly: if `borrows > 0` and `assets == reserves`, return `SCALE_1E6` (100% utilization) instead of 0, or revert so the caller can fall back to a safe static rate.
findings.title: Zero utilization returned when reserves equal assets

findings.description:
In test/debug (or when the `test-default-admin` feature is enabled), `expected_admin_config()` falls back to `DEFAULT_INIT_ADMIN` if `JUMP_RATE_MODEL_INIT_ADMIN` is unset. If this build configuration is mistakenly deployed to production, the contract’s initialization admin becomes a publicly known hardcoded address, creating a deployment-takeover (if the key is controlled) or permanent misconfiguration/DoS (if not).

Exploit path: on a misbuilt deployment, an attacker controlling the hardcoded key can front-run initialization and become admin; otherwise, the intended deployer cannot initialize the contract at all.
findings.recommendation: Remove the fallback to `DEFAULT_INIT_ADMIN` outside of unit tests, or gate it behind a compile-time flag that cannot be enabled in release builds. Consider emitting the expected admin as a deployment-time constant in tooling rather than in-contract fallback logic.
findings.title: Debug/test builds may allow hardcoded init admin

findings.description:
`withdraw_with_cash_policy` normally pays `underlying_to_return = ptoken_amount * exchange_rate / 1e6` (floor division), but if the withdrawal makes `total_supply` exactly zero it switches to a special `final_exit` payout of `get_total_underlying()` (the exact remaining supplier-owned value). Because the exchange rate is computed with only 1e6 precision and is truncated (`scaled_underlying / total_ptokens`), the “non-final” path can underpay a near-total withdrawal by a potentially non-trivial remainder, which is then captured entirely by whoever is the final redeemer.

An attacker can front-run a user who is about to withdraw the entire pToken supply by depositing a minimal amount to mint a tiny pToken balance, making the victim’s withdrawal a non-final exit (rounded down), then immediately withdrawing last to receive the full remaining `get_total_underlying()` remainder. This is a deterministic MEV/value-extraction opportunity that transfers rounding dust from the victim (and earlier redeemers) to the attacker.
findings.recommendation: Avoid giving the entire rounding remainder to the final redeemer. Options: (1) use a higher-precision exchange rate (e.g., 1e18) and consistent rounding; (2) always compute withdrawal amounts from proportional share of total underlying with full precision and explicit remainder handling; (3) keep any remainder as protocol reserves (or distribute via an accumulator) instead of paying it to the last withdrawer; and/or (4) add user-provided `min_underlying_out` bounds to protect against unexpected underpayment.
findings.title: Last-withdraw rounding can be frontrun
